Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 62, verse 1:

﴿Glorifies Allah whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth, the King, the Holy, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾

The opening of the surah with the report of the glorification of the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth for Allah, exalted is He, is an excellent opening (bara'at istihlal), because the primary purpose of the surah is to exhort attendance at the Friday prayer (Jumu'ah), to forbid the occupations that distract from attending it, and to rebuke a group of Muslims who left the Friday prayer out of eagerness to buy from a caravan (' ir) that had arrived in Medina at the time they were present for the Friday prayer.

To draw attention to the fact that the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth renew their glorification of Allah and do not slacken in it, the present tense was chosen in His saying (yusabbihu) ("glorifies").

The meanings of this verse have already been discussed separately at the beginning of Surat al-Hadid and Surat al-Hashr.

Except that in this surah the verb of glorification came in the present tense, whereas it came in the past tense elsewhere, for a reason pertaining to this place: the purpose of this surah is to highlight the Friday prayer and to censure a group who were cut off from their prayer and went out for trade or amusement. So it is fitting that the glorification of the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth be related in a form that indicates the continuity and renewal of their glorification, as an allusion to those who did not complete the Friday prayer.

The meanings of the attributes of Allah, exalted is He, mentioned here have already been discussed at the end of Surat al-Hashr.

The reason for combining these attributes here is that the Great does not allow those who are in His presence to turn away from His assembly except at the dispersal of His assembly or at His giving them leave to depart.

Al-Quddus: the One free of any deficiency, and He desires to be in His presence. Al-'Aziz: those gathered around Him gain might (ya'tazzu). So their separation from His presence is a neglect of might. Likewise al-Hakim: whenever anyone separates from His presence, he misses at every moment some portion of wisdom, just as those who dispersed toward the caravan missed what the Prophet (ﷺ) delivered in the sermon when they left him standing during the khutbah.

**[Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur, al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr, on Surah 62, verse 2]**

﴿He it is Who raised among the unlettered ones a messenger from among them, who recites to them His verses, purifies them, and teaches them the Book and wisdom, though before that they were certainly in clear error.﴾

This is a resumptive clause of explanation (*istiʾnāf bayānī*, a sentence that answers an implied question) arising from the previous attributes being predicated of the Name of Majesty (*ismu al-jalāl*, Allah). The listener may ask why these particular attributes were mentioned out of all the attributes of God, Exalted is He. The context therefore required that a great matter be explained: how these attributes relate to the conditions of His creatures, Exalted is He, in that He sent among them a messenger who purifies their souls, purifies them, and teaches them. The attribute of *al-Malik* (the King) relates to His managing the affairs of His servants and setting right their circumstances. The attribute of *al-Quddūs* (the Holy) relates to His purifying their souls. The attribute of *al-ʿAzīz* (the Mighty) requires that He join the unlettered among His servants to the ranks of the people of knowledge, and bring them out of the humiliation of error, so that they attain the might and honour of knowledge. The attribute of *al-Ḥakīm* (the Wise) requires that He teach them wisdom and the sharīʿah.

The beginning of the sentence with the pronoun of the Name of Majesty makes it a nominal sentence (*jumlah ismiyyah*), which conveys the strengthening and emphasis of this judgment, meaning that the Prophet ﷺ was indeed sent by Allah without doubt.

The *min* in His words ﴿among the unlettered ones﴾ is for *ẓarfiyyah* (indicating a container or location), meaning the *ẓarfiyyah* of the group and of one of its members. What is understood from the sense of location is the meaning of constant presence: a messenger who does not leave them. He is not passing by them as a messenger passes by with a message or a single statement that he conveys to a people and then departs from them.

The meaning is that Allah established His Messenger for the people among the Arabs, calling them and spreading his message to all people from the lands of the Arabs. The evidences that the message of Muhammad ﷺ is universal are known from other passages of the Qur'an, as in Surah al-Aʿrāf: ﴿Say: O mankind, I am the Messenger of Allah to you all﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 158], and in Surah Saba': ﴿And We have not sent you except comprehensively to mankind, as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ [Saba': 28].

By *al-unlettered ones* (*al-ummiyyīn*) is meant the Arabs, because the attribute of being unlettered was dominant among the Arab nation at that time. The description of the Messenger as *from among them* (*minhum*) means that he was not a stranger to them, as Lot was sent to the people of Sodom, or as Jonah was sent to the people of Nineveh, or as Elijah (Ilyās) was sent to the people of Sidon among the Canaanites who worshipped Baal. So *min* here is *tabʿīḍiyyah* (partitive), meaning a messenger from among the Arabs.

This is a favour directed to the Arabs, so that they may give thanks for Allah's blessing and His kindness to them. For the fact that the messenger of a people is from among them is an added blessing beyond the blessing of guidance. This is also the fulfilment of Abraham's supplication when he said: ﴿Our Lord, and raise up among them a messenger from among them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 129]. So reminding them of this blessing serves to calm their restless souls and their obstinacy.

In it there is also a *tawarruk* (a subtle rebuke, a veiled reproach) directed at them, since they turned away from hearing the Qur'an. For the fact that the Messenger is from among them and his Book is in their language is more helpful for receiving guidance from him, since it speaks to them in their tongue and directs them toward what reforms their character, so that they may become the bearers of this religion to others.

*Al-ummiyyīn* is a description of an implied noun, indicated by the form of the plural of rational beings: that is, *among the unlettered people* (*fī al-nās al-ummiyyīn*). The masculine plural form mentioned in the speech of the Lawgiver includes women by way of the technical predominance of the masculine (*taghlīb iṣṭilāḥī*, the convention of grammatically masculine forms covering both sexes), meaning *the unlettered men and the unlettered women*. For the evidences of the sharīʿah establish that its rulings cover men and women alike, except in specific known rulings.

*Al-ummiyyūn* are those who do not read or write. It is the plural of *ummī*, a nisba (relative adjective) referring to *al-ummah* (the nation), by which they mean the nation of the Arabs, because they rarely wrote. This comparison became so predominant in the usage of the Arabs that the term came to be applied to anyone who does not write, even if he is not an Arab. Allah, Exalted is He, said in mentioning the Children of Israel: ﴿And among them are unlettered ones who know not the Book except wishful fancies﴾ [al-Baqarah: 78], and this has already been discussed in Surah al-Baqarah.

The expression was chosen here as a *tawarruk* directed at the Jews, because they used it with the intent of belittling the Arabs and the Prophet ﷺ, out of ignorance. They would say: "He is the messenger of the unlettered, not a messenger to us." Ibn Ṣayyād said to the Prophet ﷺ when he said to him: "Do you bear witness that I am the Messenger of Allah?" he replied: "I bear witness that you are the messenger of the unlettered." Ibn Ṣayyād was adhering to Judaism, because his family were allies of the Jews.

The Jews would also disparage the Muslims by calling them unlettered. Allah said: ﴿That is because they said: "There is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered"﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 75]. So Allah challenged the Jews by informing them that He sent a messenger to the unlettered, and that the Messenger is unlettered. He also informed them that this is the bounty of Allah, which He gives to whom He wills, as stated at the end of the verse, and that the bounty of Allah is not restricted to the Jews or to anyone else. Allah had already said to Moses: ﴿And We wished to bestow favour upon those who were oppressed in the land, and to make them leaders and make them the inheritors, and to establish them in the land﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 5].

The description of the Messenger as *from among them*, that is, from among the unlettered, includes his similarity to them in being unlettered and in belonging to their people. This is one of the wondrous brevities of the Qur'an.

In describing the unlettered Messenger as one who recites to the unlettered the verses of Allah, that is, His revelation, and purifies them, and teaches them *al-kitāb*, that is, teaches them it by way of instruction, just as the messengers used to teach their nations the Book through writing, and teaches them wisdom, which the earlier messengers taught their nations: in all these attributes there is a challenge through the miracle of his unlettered state, peace be upon him. That is, despite being unlettered, he brought his nation all the benefits that the non-unlettered messengers brought to their nations, and he fell short of them in nothing. Thus the unlettered state became purely a miracle, since what came from its bearer was better than what came from the literate messengers, such as Moses.

In describing the unlettered one with recitation, teaching of the Book and wisdom, and purification of souls, there is a kind of *muḥassin al-ṭibāq* (the rhetorical device of antithesis), because it is well known that these are opposites of being unlettered.

Recitation was mentioned first because the first delivery of the call is the conveying of the revelation. Purification was mentioned second because the beginning of the call is purification from moral uncleanness, which is polytheism, and what clings to it of evil deeds and dispositions.

He followed this with the mention of teaching them the Book, because after the Book has been conveyed to them, its aims and meanings become clear to them, as Allah said: ﴿So when We have recited it, follow its recitation. Then upon Us is its explanation﴾ [al-Qiyāmah: 18], and He said: ﴿That you may make clear to the people what has been sent down to them﴾ [al-Naḥl: 44]. The teaching of wisdom is the goal of all of this, because whoever reflects upon the Qur'an and acts upon it, and understands its hidden meanings, attains wisdom. Allah said: ﴿And remember Allah's blessing upon you, and what He sent down to you of the Book and wisdom, by which He admonishes you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 231]. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Certainly did Allah confer favour upon the believers when He sent among them a messenger from themselves, reciting to them His verses, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and wisdom, though before that they were certainly in clear error﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 164], in Surah Āl ʿImrān.

The clause ﴿though before that they were certainly in clear error﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) relative to the unlettered ones. That is, the blessing of sending this Messenger to them is not limited to removing deficiencies from them and adorning them with the perfection of knowledge of the verses of Allah, the purification of their souls, and teaching them the Book and wisdom. Rather, it is greater than that, for it rescued them from the clear error in which they were, which was the error of associating partners with Allah. It was a clear error because it is the most foul of errors, and decisive proofs have been established against its wickedness. That is, He brought them out from manifest error to the best guidance. These are the Muslims who embraced Islam at the time this surah was revealed.

*In* (*inn*) here is a lightened form of the heavy *inna* (*mukhaffafah min al-thaqīlah*), and it is left inoperative regarding its subject and predicate. The verb *kāna* has taken its place, as is the usual usage of the lightened *in*. The *lām* in His words ﴿certainly in clear error﴾ is called *al-lām al-fāriqah* (the distinguishing *lām*), meaning the *lām* that makes a distinction between the negative *in* and the lightened *in* from the heavy form. It is nothing other than the *lām* which by origin accompanies the predicate of *inna*, since the original is: "and indeed they were in clear error." However, mention of the *lām* with the lightened form is generally obligatory, lest it be confused with the negative *in*, unless confusion is safe from occurring.

This commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 62, verse 3:

﴿And others from among them, who have not yet joined them. And He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾

It is not permissible for *wa-akharīna* (and others) to be coordinated (*'aṭf*, grammatical conjunction) with *al-ummiyyīn* (the unlettered), because *akharīna* (others) requires difference from what it is opposed to. It therefore requires that it apply to other than the *ummiyyīn*, that is, other than the Arabs. The Messenger ﷺ was not among non-Arabs, so it is determined that *wa-akharīna* should not be coordinated with *al-ummiyyīn*. Nor should it be coordinated with the pronoun in *minhum* (from among them), for the same reason.

Rather, it is either coordinated with the pronoun in *'alayhim* (upon them) in His saying ﴿He recites to them﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 2], and the sense is: "He recites to others." If he recites to them, then it is known that he was sent to them, because the recitation of the Messenger ﷺ is only a recitation of conveying what was revealed to him.

[Page 211]

Or *wa-akharīna* is made an object of accompaniment (*maf'ūl ma'ahu*), where the *wāw* indicates accompaniment (*lil-ma'iyya*), and it is governed by the three verbs: *yatlū* (recites), *yuzakkī* (purifies), and *yu'allim* (teaches). The sense is: "He recites to the unlettered His verses, purifies them, and teaches them the Book and the Wisdom, along with others."

The clause ﴿And indeed they were before in manifest error﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 2] is a parenthetical insertion between the coordinated element and that which it is coordinated with, or between the pronouns and the object of accompaniment.

*Akharīna* is the plural of *ākhar*, which means different in some attribute indicated by the context. Since *akharīna* has here been made opposite to *al-ummiyyīn*, it is meant to refer to others than the *ummiyyīn*, that is, others from among non-Arabs who are intended by "the *ummiyyīn*."

If we take the difference to be a difference in time or place, that is, "different from those among whom the Messenger was sent," and we make His saying *minhum* (from among them) mean that they are from the *ummiyyīn*, and we say the intended meaning is: "and others from among the Arabs, other than those among whom the Prophet ﷺ was, that is, other Arabs besides the people of Makkah, namely the remaining Arab tribes," this is confirmed by what al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Tirmidhi narrated, with Yazid's version (the last of them is greater than the first), from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "We were sitting with the Prophet ﷺ when the surah of al-Jumu'ah was revealed to him, and he recited it. When he reached ﴿And others from among them, who have not yet joined them﴾, a man said to him: 'Who are they, O Messenger of Allah?' He did not answer him until he had asked three times. Salman al-Farisi was among us, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ placed his hand on Salman and said: 'If faith were at the Pleiades, men from these would attain it.'" This is cited as an explanation of His saying, "and others."

What appears is that this is an explanation by a particular instance, by way of example, to convey that *akharīna* applies to many nations, among them the people of Persia. As for its inclusion of the Arab tribes, that is more fitting, because they are among those included by the word *ummiyyīn*.

Next, we should consider the interpretation of His saying *minhum* (from among them). We say: *min* may be partitive (*tab'īḍiyya*), as is most evident from its meanings. Then the pronoun governed by *min* refers to what the pronoun in *kānū* (they were) in His saying ﴿And indeed they were before in manifest error﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 2] refers to. The meaning is: "And others from among the misguided, he recites to them the signs of Allah, purifies them, and teaches them the Book and the Wisdom." We may also take *min* to be connective (*ittiṣāliyya*), like that in His saying ﴿You have no part of them in anything﴾ [al-An'am: 159]. The meaning is: "And others who join them and become part of their group." Then His saying *minhum* is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). This interpretation fits His saying ﴿who have not yet joined them﴾, because joining (*luḥūq*) is the meaning of connection.

The clause ﴿who have not yet joined them﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause. From this meaning there arises an indication that the nations who enter Islam after the first Muslims will become like them. From it there also arises a symbolic indication that they will become Arabized in understanding the religion and in reciting the Qur'an. How many sublime meanings this verse contains that the commentators have passed over in silence!

This is an unseen glad tiding that the call of the Prophet ﷺ would reach nations that are not Arabs: Persia, Armenia, the Kurds, the Berbers, the Sudanese, the Romans, the Turks, the Tatars, the Mongols, the Chinese, the Indians, and others. This is one of the miracles of the Qur'an, of the kind that reports unseen matters.

In the verse there is evidence that the mission of the Prophet ﷺ is general for all nations.

Negation with *lammā* (not yet) requires that what is negated by it continues to be unrealized up to the time of speaking, so it indicates that it is awaited to be realized, as in His saying ﴿And faith has not yet entered your hearts﴾ [al-Hujurat: 14], that is, "and it will enter," as in al-Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari). The meaning is that these others, at the time this verse was revealed, had not entered Islam and had not joined those among the Arabs who had embraced it, and they would enter in other times.

Know that the saying of the Prophet ﷺ, "If faith were with the Pleiades, men from these would attain it," is an indication of an example of what His saying ﴿and others from among them﴾ encompasses. This is because in answer to the questioner he did not state anything with a word that would require restricting the meaning of *akharīna* to the people of Salman. It is narrated from Ikrimah that they are the Followers (*tābi'ūn*). It is narrated from Mujahid that they are all the people to whom Muhammad ﷺ was sent. Ibn Umar said: they are the people of Yemen.

His saying ﴿And He is the Mighty, the Wise﴾ is a concluding phrase (*tadhyīl*) expressing wonder at this divine decree concerning the spread of this religion among all nations. The Mighty is one whose power nothing overcomes, and the Wise is one whose acts proceed from a firmly ordained measure.

The demonstrative "that" refers to everything mentioned: the sending of Muhammad (ﷺ) with the signs, the purification of souls, the teaching of the Book and wisdom, and the rescue from misguidance. It also refers to the bestowal of these perfections upon the *ummiyyin* (the unlettered people, those who had no prior knowledge or scripture), and to the joining of "other" nations (*akharin*) to this favour. Thus the exclusive claim of the Jews to the Book and the Law came to an end. This is a harder blow to their pride, for they had thought it impossible that an unlettered Messenger would bring a law to an unlettered nation. It is more so when the unlettered nations joined them, although those great nations had been more capable in knowledge and power.

And He said: ﴿Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God, that anyone should be given what you were given, or that they should argue with you before your Lord. Say: Indeed, bounty is in the hand of God; He gives it to whom He wills, and God is all-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾ [Al 'Imran: 73], which is specific to Him. This is a preface and introduction to His words, exalted is He, ﴿The likeness of those who were charged with the Torah﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 5], and the verses that follow.

The Qur'an passage (62:5) reads: ﴿The likeness of those who were entrusted with the Torah, then did not carry it, is like the likeness of a donkey carrying books. Wretched is the likeness of the people who denied the signs of Allah. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

After it became clear that He, exalted is He, had bestowed His bounty upon an unlettered people, He followed this by stating that He had also bestowed His bounty upon the People of the Book, yet these people did not benefit from it. They were satisfied with a knowledge that consisted only of carrying the Torah without understanding it. They imagined that storing the volumes of the Torah and moving them from house to house was enough to boast of it and to belittle those who did not have the Torah in their possession. The intended reference is therefore the Jews who opposed the call of Muhammad (ﷺ) and supported the polytheists.

Allah has struck a likeness for these people through the condition of a donkey that carries books, from which it gains nothing except the burden itself, without knowledge or understanding.

That is because the Jews' knowledge of what is in the Torah was mixed with additions that turned it into something tainted with errors and misguidance. They followed in it the desires of their souls and whatever would not exceed their worldly benefit. They did not adorn themselves with what it contains of guidance and of the call to purifying the soul. They also concealed what their books contain of the covenant to follow the Prophet who would come to rescue them from the noose of error. This is the connection of this verse with the verses that precede it, and for this reason it serves as a completion of what came before.

In al-Kashshaf, [al-Zamakhshari] said, on the authority of some of them: The Jews boasted that they were people of a Book, while the Arabs had no Book. So Allah refuted that claim by likening them to a donkey carrying books.

[Page 214]

The meaning of ḥummilū (﴿حُمِّلُوا﴾, "were entrusted"): the covenant was committed to them and they were charged with what it contains, but they did not fulfil what they were charged with. It is said: "I entrusted so-and-so with such-and-such a matter, and he bore it." Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We offered the trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they refused to bear it and feared it, and man bore it. Indeed, he was a wrongdoer, ignorant.﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 72].

The use of the verb "to carry" (ḥamal) and its derivatives in this sense is a metaphor (istiʿārah), by likening the entrusting of a matter to the loading of a burden onto the back of a beast. For this reason, the depiction of their condition by the condition of a donkey carrying books is a representation of the figurative meaning through a literal meaning. This is one of the subtleties of the Qur'an.

The particle thumma (﴿ثُمَّ﴾, "then") indicates a gradation in rank, since their failure to fulfil what was entrusted to them is more remarkable than their having taken it up. The clause ﴿yaḥmilu asfāran﴾ ("carrying books") is either in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the donkey, or in the position of a descriptive clause (ṣifah), because the definiteness of "the donkey" here is generic: it is definite in form but indefinite in meaning. Therefore, both the circumstantial and the descriptive interpretations are valid for the clause.

This likeness is intended to express the vileness of their condition, and it is an instance of likening an intelligible matter to a sensible, familiar one. For this reason it is followed by a censure of their condition: ﴿Wretched is the likeness of the people who denied the signs of Allah.﴾

The word bi'sa (﴿بِئْسَ﴾, "wretched") is a verb of blame, meaning: evil is the condition of those who denied the Book of Allah. They combined with their ignorance of the meanings of the Torah a denial of the signs of Allah, which are the Qur'an.

The phrase ﴿mathalu l-qawmi﴾ ("the likeness of the people") is the subject (fā'il) of bi'sa. The subject has taken the place of mention of the object of blame, because it is known that what is condemned is the condition of the people who deny. So this construction did not follow the mode of ambiguity that requires explanation, since what it explains has already been stated by the likeness mentioned before it, in His words ﴿like the likeness of a donkey carrying books﴾. Hence repeating the word "likeness" would have made the speech heavy, being used more than three times. This is one of the varieties of Qur'anic expression. The clause ﴿alladhina kadhdhabu﴾ ("who denied") is a descriptive clause (ṣifah) of "the people."

The clause ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyīl) informing about them that the evil of their condition holds no prospect of their being freed from it, because Allah has deprived them of kindness and of the care that would have rescued them, on account of their wrongdoing in transgressing against the Messenger (ﷺ) by denial without reflection, and against the signs of Allah by rejection without contemplation.

In al-Kashshaf: "And on the authority of some of them: Allah has refuted the claim of the Jews in three matters," meaning three verses of this surah. They boasted that they were the friends and beloved of Allah, so He refuted them in His words: ﴿So wish for death, if you are truthful﴾ [Al-Jumu'ah: 6].
