Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 62, verse 6:

﴿Say, "O you who are Jews, if you claim that you are allies of Allah to the exclusion of the [rest of] people, then wish for death, if you should be truthful."﴾

He follows the depiction of their ignorance of the Torah with mention of a claim that is among the effects of their ignorance of it, refuting a supposed boast they held: that they are the allies of Allah and that the rest of mankind is not like them. This was a principle they used as proof that their affairs were superior to the affairs of others. Among this is that they used to boast that Allah had given them the Sabbath, the best day of the week, and that the Gentiles (al-ummiyyun) did not have anything like it. So when Allah made Friday (al-Jumu'ah) for the Muslims, they were enraged. In al-Kashshaf: the Jews boasted of the Sabbath and that the Muslims did not have anything like it, so Allah legislated Friday for them.

It is opened with the verb "qul" (say) for emphasis (li-l-ihtimam).

And "alladhina hadu" (those who are Jews): these are the ones who were Jews. The reason for naming the Jews "Yahud" was discussed at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who were Jews﴾ [al-Baqarah: 62] in Surat al-Baqarah. It is possible that "hadu" means "repented," in reference to the saying of Musa, upon him be peace, after the earthquake seized them: ﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You﴾ [al-A'raf: 156], as was mentioned in Surat al-A'raf. The most common description of the Children of Israel in the Qur'an is that they are "Hud," the plural of "ha'id" like "qu'ud" as the plural of "qa'id." The origin of "Hud" is "Hawud," and this meaning has been forgotten from it and it became a proper name through predominance over the Children of Israel, so they are addressed by it here in this sense, because the context is not one of praise for them, or it is sarcasm.

The conditional "in" (in) is used, whose basic function is non-certainty of the occurrence of the condition, although the condition here is certain to occur, since they are well known for this claim, and the Qur'an recounts it about them in Surat al-Ma'idah:

﴿The Jews and the Christians said, "We are the children of Allah and His beloved."﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18]. This is to indicate that since their claim is false by the evidence, it is treated as something whose occurrence is supposed, just as something unlikely is supposed, as if it were not actually occurring, in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Shall We then withhold the reminder from you, turning away, because you are a transgressing people?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 5]. This conveys reproach by way of implication (kinayah).

The meaning is: if you are truthful in your claim, then wish for death. This is a compulsion upon them so that the establishment of their doubt regarding what they claimed becomes binding upon them.

The imperative in His saying "fatamannaw" (then wish) is used to express incapacitation (al-ta'jiz), as a metaphor (kinayah) for denial, like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Say, "Bring the Torah and recite it, if you should be truthful."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 93].

The connection between the condition and its answer is that death is the return of a person with his soul to an eternal life in which the effects of Allah's pleasure with the servant or His anger become manifest, so that He may recompense him according to his deeds.

The conclusion that follows from this condition establishes that they are like all people in the two lives, this world and the Hereafter, and their effects, and the differing states of their people in each, so it is known from this that they are not superior to other people. This is what His saying, Exalted is He, indicates: ﴿The Jews and the Christians said, "We are the children of Allah and His beloved." Say, "Then why does He punish you for your sins? Rather, you are human beings from among those He has created."﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18].

By this, the objection that may occur to the reader of this verse is dispelled, namely its apparent conflict with the sound reports prohibiting the wishing for death. It is reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever loves to meet Allah, Allah loves to meet him, and whoever hates to meet Allah, Allah hates to meet him." Then 'A'ishah said: "We dislike death." He said to her: "It is not that." (the hadith). And it is reported from him that he said: "The Angel of Death was sent to Musa, and when he came to him, he struck him, so he returned to his Lord and said, 'You sent me to a servant who does not want death,' up to his saying, Musa said, 'Now then.'"

That is because the condition of the believers is to be between hope and fear of Allah, and they do not imagine that success is guaranteed for them, as the Jews imagined.

What this verse contains, as a report about the state of the Jews present at that time, who were a general group overwhelmed by delusion and deception after the passing of their scholars, is a description of a collective people. As for the reports we cited, they describe specific states and specific individuals, so there is no contradiction given the difference of states and times. If anyone had certain knowledge of hastening to bliss, he would wish for death, unless his life was for the support of the religion, like the life of the prophets.

Upon the first, the state of 'Umayr ibn al-Humam is understood, in his saying:

"Rushing toward Allah without provision."

And the state of Ja'far ibn Abi Talib on the day of Mu'tah, when he broke into the ranks of the polytheists:

"O how excellent is Paradise, and its nearness..."

And the saying of 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah:

"But I ask the Most Merciful for forgiveness, and a blow with a wide wound that spills the foam,"

which was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Baqarah, because martyrdom has a guaranteed best reward and complete forgiveness.

Upon the second is understood the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to 'A'ishah, in interpretation of his saying "Whoever loves to meet Allah, Allah loves to meet him": that when death comes to the believer, he is given the good news of Allah's pleasure, so nothing is more beloved to him than what lies ahead, and so he loves meeting Allah. And the saying of Musa, upon him be peace, to the Angel of Death: "Now then."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 62, verse 7:

﴿And they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have put forward. And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers.﴾

This is an interjection between the two statements of speech, intended to challenge them and to establish the proof against them that they are not the allies of Allah.

The purpose here is not to offer them an excuse for not wishing for death; rather, the purpose is to further expose the falsehood of their claim, ﴿We are the sons of Allah and His beloved﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18], and to establish that they are in doubt about this, as the Qur'an's argument against them indicates by their certainty that Allah punishes them for their sins, in His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And the Jews and the Christians said, "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved." Say, "Then why does He punish you for your sins?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18]. This has already been discussed in the tafsir of Surah al-'Uqud (al-Ma'idah).

The ba' (ب) in ﴿because of what their hands have put forward﴾ is causal (sababiyyah), connected to the negated verb (yatamannawnahu, "they wish for it"). So what their hands have put forward is the cause of their not wishing for death: it cast fear into their souls because of what their hands had put forward. Thus it was the reason for their being turned away from wishing for death, due to the proof having preceded them.

Ma (ما) is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), and the returning pronoun of the relative clause is omitted; its omission is the more common usage in such constructions.

"Hands" (al-aydi) is a metaphor for the acquisition of deeds, because the hand is generally associated with acquiring. What is meant by "what their hands have put forward" are their evil deeds and their disobediences, by the indication of the context.

A parallel to this verse has already occurred in Surah al-Baqarah, and what I have mentioned here is more complete than what was said there, so I combine the two.

Taqdim (التقديم, "putting forward") originally means making a thing precede, i.e., placing it ahead of others in a place where they will come after it. It is used here, metaphorically, for the deeds that have already passed, likening them to a thing that a person precedes to a place before arriving there himself.

As for the phrase ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾, meaning: He knows their conditions and the conditions of their like among the wrongdoers. The word "the wrongdoers" thus includes the Jews, for they are among the wrongdoers. The meaning of their wrongdoing has already been mentioned in the preceding verse. The Jews have been described as wrongdoers in many verses, and this was discussed at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from Allah?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 140]. The intent is that their holding back from wishing for death is due to the fear of punishment in their souls for what they did in the world. So knowledge of Allah of their conditions is alluded to as a means of indicating that they will not escape the recompense for them, and in this there is a warning to them.

**Page 219**

This is an explicit statement of what the concluding clause (*tadhyil*, a closing phrase that reinforces the point) implied: the threat that they cannot escape the recompense for their deeds, even if a long time passes before those deeds occur. The length of time does not make God's knowledge forgetful, since He is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed. The position of this sentence is that of a *badal al-ishtimal* (a substitute that includes what it replaces) relative to the clause ﴿فَتَمَنَّوُا المَوْتَ إنْ كُنْتُمْ صادِقِينَ﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 6], meaning "then wish for death, if you are truthful." The repetition of the verb ﴿قُلْ﴾ ("Say") is of the same kind as the repetition of the governing verb in the substituted element, as in God's words ﴿تَكُونُ لَنا عِيدًا لِأوَّلِنا وآخِرِنا﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 114], meaning "a feast for the first of us and the last of us," in Surat al-'Uqud.

He described death as ﴿الَّذِي تَفِرُّونَ مِنهُ﴾ ("that from which you flee") to draw attention to the fact that their panic at death is a mistake, as in the words of 'Alqamah:

*Indeed those you see as your brothers,*
*whose hearts' thirst would be quenched by your being struck down.*

He used the word "flight" for intense caution, by way of metaphor (*isti'ara*).

The attaching of the predicate of *inna* with the letter *fa'* in His words ﴿فَإنَّهُ مُلاقِيكُمْ﴾ ("for indeed it will meet you") is because the subject of *inna* is qualified by a relative pronoun (*ism al-mawsul*), and the relative clause is often treated like a conditional (*shart*). So the subject of *inna*, qualified by the relative clause, is treated in the same way as its qualifier.

The repetition of the first *inna* serves to add emphasis, as in the words of Jarir:

*Indeed the caliph, indeed God has clothed him*
*in a garment of kingship, by which outcomes are hoped for.*

This was discussed earlier at His words ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وعَمِلُوا الصّالِحاتِ إنّا لا نُضِيعُ أجْرَ مَن أحْسَنَ عَمَلًا﴾ [al-Kahf: 30] in Surat al-Kahf, and also in Surat al-Hajj.

The phrase ﴿فَيُنَبِّئُكم بِما كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ ("then He will inform you of what you used to do") is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for being held accountable for it, and it is an allusion (*ta'ridh*) to the threat.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 62, verses 9–10 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿O you who have believed, when the call is proclaimed for the prayer on the day of Friday, then proceed to the remembrance of Allah and leave off trade. That is better for you, if you only knew.﴾ ﴿And when the prayer has been concluded, disperse within the land and seek of the bounty of Allah, and remember Allah much that you may succeed.﴾

These verses are the purpose of the surah, and what precedes them is an introduction and preparation for them, as we mentioned earlier. It has already been mentioned what al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari's tafsir) reported, that the Jews boasted over the Muslims about the Sabbath, so Allah legislated Friday (al-Jumu'ah) for the Muslims. This is the connection of this verse to the four verses before it, so let this verse be a preparation and an introduction.

The *lam* in His saying *li-l-salah* ("for the prayer") is the *lam* of causation (ta'lil), meaning: a caller called out for the sake of the prayer on the day of Friday. From this it is known that the "call" here is the adhan (call to prayer).

*Al-Jumu'ah* is pronounced with a *damma* on the *jim* and a *damma* on the *mim* in the dialect of the majority of the Arabs, and it is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. The Banu 'Uqayl pronounce the *mim* with a sukun (*al-Jum'ah*).

The definiteness in *al-salah* is the definiteness of reference (ta'rif al-'ahd), and it is the well-known prayer specific to the day of Friday.

[Page 220]

It was established as a legislated practice through mass transmission (tawatur), and then it was confirmed by this verse. Thus the evidence for its obligation became the Book, the mass-transmitted Sunnah, and the consensus (ijma') of the Ummah.

The Friday prayer was legislated from the first days of the Hijrah. It is narrated from Ibn Sirin that the Ansar gathered for Friday before the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Medina. They said: "The Jews have a day on which they gather, and the Christians have a similar day. Come, let us gather until we make for ourselves a day on which we remember Allah and pray in it." They said: "The Jews have Saturday and the Christians have Sunday, so let us make it the day of 'Aruba." So they gathered at As'ad ibn Zurarah, and he prayed with them that day two rak'ahs and admonished them.

Al-Bayhaqi narrated from al-Zuhri that Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr was the first to gather for Friday in Medina before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to it. It is necessary that this was known to the Prophet (ﷺ), and perhaps they had received from the Prophet (ﷺ) the hadith about the excellence of the day of Friday and that it is the day of the Muslims.

Thus the legislation of the Friday prayer and gathering on it was an answer from Allah, the Exalted, to the desire of the Muslims, just as His answer to the desire of the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding facing the Ka'bah, mentioned in His saying: ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the sky, so We will surely turn you to a qiblah that will please you. So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144].

As for the first Friday prayer that the Prophet (ﷺ) led, the people of the biographies (ahl al-siyar) said: it was on the fifth day after the Hijrah, because the Messenger of Allah arrived in Medina on Monday, twelve nights having passed from Rabi' al-Awwal. He stayed at Quba, then went out on Friday toward Medina, and the time of the Friday prayer overtook him in the valley of Banu Salim ibn 'Awf, where they had a mosque. So he led them in prayer in that mosque, and he delivered in it the first sermon (khutbah) he gave in Medina, and it is long; al-Qurtubi mentioned its text in his tafsir.

Their saying "the time of the Friday prayer overtook him" indicates that the Friday prayer was legislated at that time, and that the Prophet (ﷺ) was determined to pray it in Medina, but the time became too tight for him, so he performed it in the mosque of Banu Salim. Then he prayed the next Friday in his mosque in Medina, and the Friday prayer of the Prophet's Mosque in Medina was the second one, according to the authentic reports.

The first Friday prayer held in a mosque among the mosques in the lands of Islam after Medina was in the mosque of Ju'atha' in the lands of Bahrain, which is the city of al-Khatt, a village of 'Abd al-Qays. When the Arabs apostatized after the death of the Prophet (ﷺ), the people of Ju'atha' remained steadfast upon Islam.

It is established that Friday is the seventh day of the week in Islam, and it is the one that was called 'Aruba in the Jahiliyyah. Some scholars said: "It is not preceded by the definite article (al-)." Al-Suhayli said: "The meaning of 'Aruba is rest, as has reached me from some of the people of knowledge." I say: this is narrated from Tha'lab, and it was the day before Saturday. Saturday was the festival of the week for the Jews, and it is the last day of the week. Rest from work was prescribed for them on it by the text of the Torah, so they began counting the days of the week from Sunday, which comes right after Saturday. The Arabs followed them in this for reasons that are not known. For this reason the early Arabs named Sunday (*awwal*, "first").

So the names of the days of the week among the Arabs in ancient times were: *Awwal*; *Ahwan*; *Jubar* (like *ghurab* and *kitab*); *Dubar* in the same pattern; *Mu'ays* (with hamza); *'Aruba*; *Shiyar* with a kasrah on the *shin* followed by a light *ya*.

Then they introduced names for these days, which are: al-Ahad (Sunday), al-Ithnayn (Monday), al-Thulatha' (Tuesday, with the first *tha'* pronounced with fatha or damma), al-Irbi'a' (Wednesday, with kasrah on the hamza and kasrah on the *ba'*), al-Khamis (Thursday), 'Aruba or al-Jumu'ah (according to some of them), and al-Sabt (Saturday). The origin of *sabt* is "cutting off," and it was named *sabt* among the Israelites because they cut off work on it, and that name spread among the Arabs.

They named the four days after it by names derived from the names of the numbers in their order. The Torah does not mention names for the days. In the Book of Genesis, the days of the beginning of creation are mentioned by their numbers, "first, second," etc., and that Allah did not create anything on the day after the sixth day. The Torah named it *Sabt* (Sabbath).

Al-Suhayli said: It was said that the first to call the day of 'Aruba "Friday" was Ka'b ibn Lu'ayy, the grandfather of Abu Qusayy, and the Quraysh used to gather to Ka'b on it. He said: In the saying of some of them: the day of 'Aruba was not called Friday except since Islam came.

Allah made the day of Friday the festival of the week for the Muslims, so He legislated for them the gathering of the people of the town in the mosque and hearing the sermon, so that they would be taught what concerns them in establishing the affairs of their religion and their reform.

Al-Qaffal said: When Allah made people the most noble of the lower world, He did not conceal the greatness of the favor and the majesty of the rank of His gift to them, so He commanded them to give thanks for this honor on one of the seven days, so that their gathering on that day would be a reminder of the greatness of what Allah bestowed upon them. Every well-known religious community has a day of the week that it honors: for the Jews it is Saturday, for the Christians Sunday, and for the Muslims Friday. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "We are the last (in the world), the first on the Day of Resurrection," and "The Day of Resurrection" is connected with "the first." However, they, meaning the Jews and the Christians, were given the Book before us, then this day was the one about which they differed, so Allah guided us to it. So people are followers of us in it: the Jews tomorrow, and the Christians the day after tomorrow.

When Friday was made a day of thanks and of honoring a blessing, it was necessary to have a gathering through which its fame would spread, so congregations were gathered for it, and a sermon was needed in it as a reminder of the blessing and an incitement to its continuation. Since the basis of honoring it is the prayer, the prayer was made for this day at the middle of the day, so the gathering would be complete, and this prayer was not permitted except in one mosque, so that it would be the most effective in gathering. End of al-Qaffal's words.

The Prophet's (ﷺ) saying "and the Christians the day after tomorrow" refers to what the Christians did after Jesus and after the disciples: they replaced Saturday with Sunday, because they claimed that on Sunday 'Isa (Jesus) rose from his grave. So they substituted Sunday for Saturday by an order from Constantine, the ruler of the Romans, in the year 321 CE. It became a religion for them by the order of their rabbis.

The Friday prayer is the noon prayer (salat al-zuhr) of Friday, and it is not an extra prayer beyond the five daily prayers. Two rak'ahs were removed from the noon prayer because of the two sermons. It is narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "The Friday prayer was shortened only because of the sermon."

[Page 223]

I believe that this was a lightening upon people, since two sermons became obligatory on them along with the prayer, so each sermon was in the place of a rak'ah. This is the reason for sitting between the two sermons, as an indication that they stand in place of the two rak'ahs, and for this reason the sitting was brief. However, the two sermons were not given the rulings of the two rak'ahs, so the missing of one of them or the missing of both together does no harm, and it is not obligatory for the latecomer (masbuq) to make them up, nor is there a prostration for their omission, according to the majority of the jurists of the major cities. It is narrated from 'Ata', Mujahid, and Tawus that whoever misses the sermon on Friday prays four rak'ahs as the noon prayer. And from 'Ata': whoever catches one rak'ah of the Friday prayer adds three rak'ahs to it. He meant: if he misses the sermon and one rak'ah of the Friday prayer.

The recitation in the prayer was made aloud, although the norm for the daytime prayers is to recite quietly, for the benefit of making the people hear some surahs of the Qur'an, just as they were made to hear the sermon. So it was a prayer of guidance for the people of the town on one day of every week.

There is consensus that the Friday prayer stands in place of the noon prayer on Friday, so whoever prays it does not pray the noon prayer along with it. As for whoever did not pray it, due to an excuse or other reasons, it is obligatory upon him to pray the noon prayer. I saw in the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus that an imam stood to lead a congregation in the noon prayer after finishing the Friday prayer, and that is an innovation (bid'ah).

The jurists differed about the basic obligation at the time of the noon prayer on Friday. Malik, al-Shafi'i in his last of two opinions, Ahmad, and Zufar among the companions of Abu Hanifah said: the well-known Friday prayer is the obligation at the time of the zawal (midday) on Friday, and the noon prayer on that day is only a substitute for the Friday prayer, i.e., for one who did not pray the Friday prayer due to an excuse or the like.

Abu Hanifah, al-Shafi'i in his first opinion (which he retracted), Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad in one narration said: the obligation in origin is the noon prayer, and the Friday prayer is a substitute for the noon prayer. This is what the Hanafi jurists affirmed as correct.

Muhammad said in one narration from him: the obligation is one of the two prayers without specification, and the specification is for the mukallaf (responsible person), so it resembles the optional obligation (wajib mukhayyar), because in the optional obligation the doer of either of the two matters does not sin, while one who abandons the Friday prayer without an excuse is sinful.

[Page 224]

They said: the fruit of the disagreement appears in a free resident who prayed the noon prayer at the beginning of its time. Abu Hanifah and his companions said: he has the noon prayer absolutely, so that even if he went out after he had prayed the noon prayer, or did not go out, his obligation is not nullified. But according to Abu Hanifah his noon prayer is nullified merely by the act of striving (sa'y) absolutely, and according to his two companions his noon prayer is not nullified unless he catches the Friday prayer.

Malik and al-Shafi'i said: it is not permitted to pray the noon prayer on Friday, whether he catches the Friday prayer or not, whether he went out to it or not. That is, if he catches the Friday prayer the matter is clear, and if he does not catch it, it is obligatory upon him to pray another noon prayer.

The call to prayer (al-nida' li-l-salah) is the well-known adhan, which is the adhan for the noon prayer. It is reported in the Sahih from al-Sa'ib ibn Yazid, who said: "The call on Friday was when the imam sat on the minbar during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, and 'Umar. Al-Sa'ib ibn Yazid said: When 'Uthman came and the people in Medina increased, he added an adhan at al-Zawra'." (al-Zawra': a place in the market of Medina.) Some narrations describe it as the second adhan. The meaning of its being second is that it is a repeated adhan in addition to the original adhan, so it is second in legislation, and it does not mean that it is called after finishing the adhan that is called when the imam sits on the minbar. That is, it is called at the door of the mosque, since at that time people did not have a minaret. Some narrations describe it as the third call, and this is meant only because it is third when added to the first adhan. It does not mean that people call two adhans in the mosque; rather 'Uthman added it so that those on the outskirts of Medina would hear the call, and they sometimes called it the first adhan.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 62, verses 9–10 (part 2 of 2):

What appears from a careful examination of the reports is that this second adhan is called out immediately after the first adhan, because the purpose is for people to attend the prayer at one time. Some expressions in the reports and in the words of the narrators state that the adhan was called at al-Zawra' first, and then the imam would come out and the adhan would be given in front of him.

Ibn al-'Arabi said in al-'Aridah: When the people increased in number in the time of 'Uthman, he added a call at al-Zawra' so that the people would be aware of the time and begin to come to the Friday prayer. Then 'Uthman would come out, and when he sat on the minbar, the second adhan, which had been the first in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), was called, and then he would deliver the khutbah. Then the third adhan is called, meaning by it the iqamah. End of quote.

He also said in al-Ahkam: He called it, in the hadith of al-Sa'ib ibn Yazid, a "third," because it is an addition to the iqamah, so he made it the third of the iqamah; that is, because it was introduced after the iqamah had been legislated. He called the iqamah an adhan by way of similarity (mushakalah), or because it is a notification (iidhan) of entry into the prayer, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Between every two adhans there is a prayer for whoever wishes," meaning between the adhan and the iqamah. So people imagined that it was an original adhan, and they made the adhans three, and this was a delusion. Then they gathered them at one time, and this was a delusion upon a delusion. End of quote. Thus many people in the regions imagined that the adhan for the Friday prayer is three times. For this reason you see them calling three adhans in the mosques of Tunis, and this is an innovation (bid'ah).

Ibn al-'Arabi said in al-'Aridah: As for the Maghrib, meaning the lands of the Maghrib, three muezzins call the adhan there, due to the ignorance of the jurists. In al-Risalah: This second adhan was introduced by the Banu Umayyah, so he described it as the second, which is the verified position, but he attributed it to the Banu Umayyah because it is not established that the one who added it was 'Uthman. It was narrated by al-Bukhari and the authors of the Sunan from al-Sa'ib ibn Yazid, and Muslim did not narrate it, nor did Malik in the Muwatta'.

The reason for attributing it to the Banu Umayyah is that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, when he was in Kufa, did not call the adhan for the Friday prayer except a single adhan, as was the case in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the adhan which 'Uthman had introduced in Medina was abolished. Perhaps it was one of the caliphs of the Banu Umayyah who restored the second adhan. Malik said in al-Majmu'ah: Hisham ibn 'Abd al-Malik introduced a second adhan in front of him in the mosque.

Know that the call to which the command to strive (al-sa'y) in this verse is attached is the first call, and the second call was only a relaying of the adhan for those who were far away. Whoever hears it is obliged to strive to the Friday prayer, since he knows that a call for the Friday prayer has been made.

Al-sa'y: its original meaning is exerting oneself in walking. Here it is used for walking with eagerness and avoiding lateness, figuratively.

(Remembrance of Allah) has been interpreted as the prayer, and it has been interpreted as the khutbah. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and Sa'id ibn Jubayr explained it thus. Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: The correct view is that it includes all of it, its beginning being the khutbah.

I say: The choice of "remembrance of Allah" here, rather than saying "to the prayer," as in His saying ﴿Then when the prayer is concluded﴾, is so that both matters, the khutbah and the prayer, may be intended. In it is evidence for the obligation of the khutbah in the Friday prayer and its being a condition in general. The detailed rulings on neglecting the khutbah are not equal to those on neglecting the prayer, except in the basic prohibition of absenting oneself from attending the khutbah without an excuse.

In the hadith of the Muwatta': "When the imam comes out, the angels attend, listening to the remembrance (al-dhikr)." There is no doubt that when the imam comes out he begins with the khutbah, so the khutbah is part of the remembrance, and in this is an explanation of the word "remembrance" in this verse. They were forbidden from trading because it is what preoccupies them, and because the occasion of the revelation of the verse was that a group of them left the Friday prayer to go after a caravan of merchandise that had arrived, as will come in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And when they see a trade or amusement, they break away toward it﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 11].

Like trading is everything that preoccupies one from striving to the Friday prayer. And after trading and what is analogous to it, there has been disagreement concerning the annulment (naskh) of contracts that were concluded at the time of the Friday prayer. This is based on the disagreement over whether a prohibition necessitates the invalidity of what is prohibited. The position of Malik is that a prohibition necessitates invalidity unless there is an indication otherwise. Malik's statement in al-Mudawwanah: a sale concluded at the time of the Friday prayer between those upon whom the Friday prayer is obligatory is annulled. Al-Shafi'i said: it is not annulled, and he treated it like prayer in usurped land; this is also the view of Abu Hanifah.

As for a marriage contracted at the time of the Friday prayer: in al-'Utbiyyah from Ibn al-Qasim, it is not annulled. Perhaps he limited himself to what the prohibition was stated about in the Qur'an, and did not regard analogy as requiring the annulment of what is analogized. Likewise the leading Malikis said: a partnership, a gift, or a charity concluded at the time of the Friday prayer is not annulled, and they justified this by the rarity of the occurrence of their like, unlike sale.

The address of the verse is to all the believers, which indicates that the Friday prayer is obligatory upon each individual (fard 'ayn). A group deviated, saying it is obligatory as a communal duty (fard kifayah). Ibn al-Faras said: this was attributed to some Shafi'is. The Qur'anic address "O you who believe" is general, and the Sunnah has specified it by the non-obligation of the Friday prayer upon women, slaves, a traveler who arrives at a village where the Friday prayer is held, and whoever cannot make the effort to reach it.

The "min" in His saying (﴿from the day of Friday﴾) is partitive (tab'idiyyah), since the day of Friday is a time in which acts occur, among them the well-known prayer in it, so what occurs within the time is treated as parts of the thing. It is also permissible for "min" to be for location (zarfiyyah), like the one in His saying (﴿Show me what they have created from the earth﴾ [Fatir: 40]), meaning: in it, of earthly creatures.

The demonstrative "that" (dhalikum) refers to what has been mentioned, namely the command to strive to it and the command to leave off trading at that time; that is, that is better for you than what you gain from sales. The word "khayr" is a comparative form whose original is akhyar, its hamzah dropped due to frequent use.

The element compared against is omitted, being indicated by the context. The thing preferred is the prayer, meaning its reward. The thing compared against is the benefits of sale for seller and buyer.

It was followed by His saying, ﴿Then when the prayer is concluded, disperse in the land and seek of Allah's bounty﴾, to indicate that they have a span of the day which they may devote to sale and similar pursuits of livelihood, so they should not take that from the time of prayer and the remembrance of Allah. The command in ﴿disperse in the land and seek of Allah's bounty﴾ is for permission (ibahah).

What is meant by "Allah's bounty" is the earning of wealth and sustenance.

As for His saying, ﴿and remember Allah much﴾, it is a safeguard against being absorbed in the affairs of this world to the point of forgetting the remembrance of Allah or being distracted from the prayers, for success lies in devoting oneself to the pleasure of Allah, Exalted is He.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 62, verses 9–10 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿O you who have believed, when the call is proclaimed for the prayer on the day of Friday, then proceed to the remembrance of Allah and leave off trade. That is better for you, if you only knew.﴾ ﴿And when the prayer has been concluded, disperse within the land and seek of the bounty of Allah, and remember Allah much that you may succeed.﴾

These verses are the purpose of the surah, and what precedes them is an introduction and preparation for them, as we mentioned earlier. It has already been mentioned what al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari's tafsir) reported, that the Jews boasted over the Muslims about the Sabbath, so Allah legislated Friday (al-Jumu'ah) for the Muslims. This is the connection of this verse to the four verses before it, so let this verse be a preparation and an introduction.

The *lam* in His saying *li-l-salah* ("for the prayer") is the *lam* of causation (ta'lil), meaning: a caller called out for the sake of the prayer on the day of Friday. From this it is known that the "call" here is the adhan (call to prayer).

*Al-Jumu'ah* is pronounced with a *damma* on the *jim* and a *damma* on the *mim* in the dialect of the majority of the Arabs, and it is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. The Banu 'Uqayl pronounce the *mim* with a sukun (*al-Jum'ah*).

The definiteness in *al-salah* is the definiteness of reference (ta'rif al-'ahd), and it is the well-known prayer specific to the day of Friday.

[Page 220]

It was established as a legislated practice through mass transmission (tawatur), and then it was confirmed by this verse. Thus the evidence for its obligation became the Book, the mass-transmitted Sunnah, and the consensus (ijma') of the Ummah.

The Friday prayer was legislated from the first days of the Hijrah. It is narrated from Ibn Sirin that the Ansar gathered for Friday before the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Medina. They said: "The Jews have a day on which they gather, and the Christians have a similar day. Come, let us gather until we make for ourselves a day on which we remember Allah and pray in it." They said: "The Jews have Saturday and the Christians have Sunday, so let us make it the day of 'Aruba." So they gathered at As'ad ibn Zurarah, and he prayed with them that day two rak'ahs and admonished them.

Al-Bayhaqi narrated from al-Zuhri that Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr was the first to gather for Friday in Medina before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to it. It is necessary that this was known to the Prophet (ﷺ), and perhaps they had received from the Prophet (ﷺ) the hadith about the excellence of the day of Friday and that it is the day of the Muslims.

Thus the legislation of the Friday prayer and gathering on it was an answer from Allah, the Exalted, to the desire of the Muslims, just as His answer to the desire of the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding facing the Ka'bah, mentioned in His saying: ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the sky, so We will surely turn you to a qiblah that will please you. So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144].

As for the first Friday prayer that the Prophet (ﷺ) led, the people of the biographies (ahl al-siyar) said: it was on the fifth day after the Hijrah, because the Messenger of Allah arrived in Medina on Monday, twelve nights having passed from Rabi' al-Awwal. He stayed at Quba, then went out on Friday toward Medina, and the time of the Friday prayer overtook him in the valley of Banu Salim ibn 'Awf, where they had a mosque. So he led them in prayer in that mosque, and he delivered in it the first sermon (khutbah) he gave in Medina, and it is long; al-Qurtubi mentioned its text in his tafsir.

Their saying "the time of the Friday prayer overtook him" indicates that the Friday prayer was legislated at that time, and that the Prophet (ﷺ) was determined to pray it in Medina, but the time became too tight for him, so he performed it in the mosque of Banu Salim. Then he prayed the next Friday in his mosque in Medina, and the Friday prayer of the Prophet's Mosque in Medina was the second one, according to the authentic reports.

The first Friday prayer held in a mosque among the mosques in the lands of Islam after Medina was in the mosque of Ju'atha' in the lands of Bahrain, which is the city of al-Khatt, a village of 'Abd al-Qays. When the Arabs apostatized after the death of the Prophet (ﷺ), the people of Ju'atha' remained steadfast upon Islam.

It is established that Friday is the seventh day of the week in Islam, and it is the one that was called 'Aruba in the Jahiliyyah. Some scholars said: "It is not preceded by the definite article (al-)." Al-Suhayli said: "The meaning of 'Aruba is rest, as has reached me from some of the people of knowledge." I say: this is narrated from Tha'lab, and it was the day before Saturday. Saturday was the festival of the week for the Jews, and it is the last day of the week. Rest from work was prescribed for them on it by the text of the Torah, so they began counting the days of the week from Sunday, which comes right after Saturday. The Arabs followed them in this for reasons that are not known. For this reason the early Arabs named Sunday (*awwal*, "first").

So the names of the days of the week among the Arabs in ancient times were: *Awwal*; *Ahwan*; *Jubar* (like *ghurab* and *kitab*); *Dubar* in the same pattern; *Mu'ays* (with hamza); *'Aruba*; *Shiyar* with a kasrah on the *shin* followed by a light *ya*.

Then they introduced names for these days, which are: al-Ahad (Sunday), al-Ithnayn (Monday), al-Thulatha' (Tuesday, with the first *tha'* pronounced with fatha or damma), al-Irbi'a' (Wednesday, with kasrah on the hamza and kasrah on the *ba'*), al-Khamis (Thursday), 'Aruba or al-Jumu'ah (according to some of them), and al-Sabt (Saturday). The origin of *sabt* is "cutting off," and it was named *sabt* among the Israelites because they cut off work on it, and that name spread among the Arabs.

They named the four days after it by names derived from the names of the numbers in their order. The Torah does not mention names for the days. In the Book of Genesis, the days of the beginning of creation are mentioned by their numbers, "first, second," etc., and that Allah did not create anything on the day after the sixth day. The Torah named it *Sabt* (Sabbath).

Al-Suhayli said: It was said that the first to call the day of 'Aruba "Friday" was Ka'b ibn Lu'ayy, the grandfather of Abu Qusayy, and the Quraysh used to gather to Ka'b on it. He said: In the saying of some of them: the day of 'Aruba was not called Friday except since Islam came.

Allah made the day of Friday the festival of the week for the Muslims, so He legislated for them the gathering of the people of the town in the mosque and hearing the sermon, so that they would be taught what concerns them in establishing the affairs of their religion and their reform.

Al-Qaffal said: When Allah made people the most noble of the lower world, He did not conceal the greatness of the favor and the majesty of the rank of His gift to them, so He commanded them to give thanks for this honor on one of the seven days, so that their gathering on that day would be a reminder of the greatness of what Allah bestowed upon them. Every well-known religious community has a day of the week that it honors: for the Jews it is Saturday, for the Christians Sunday, and for the Muslims Friday. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "We are the last (in the world), the first on the Day of Resurrection," and "The Day of Resurrection" is connected with "the first." However, they, meaning the Jews and the Christians, were given the Book before us, then this day was the one about which they differed, so Allah guided us to it. So people are followers of us in it: the Jews tomorrow, and the Christians the day after tomorrow.

When Friday was made a day of thanks and of honoring a blessing, it was necessary to have a gathering through which its fame would spread, so congregations were gathered for it, and a sermon was needed in it as a reminder of the blessing and an incitement to its continuation. Since the basis of honoring it is the prayer, the prayer was made for this day at the middle of the day, so the gathering would be complete, and this prayer was not permitted except in one mosque, so that it would be the most effective in gathering. End of al-Qaffal's words.

The Prophet's (ﷺ) saying "and the Christians the day after tomorrow" refers to what the Christians did after Jesus and after the disciples: they replaced Saturday with Sunday, because they claimed that on Sunday 'Isa (Jesus) rose from his grave. So they substituted Sunday for Saturday by an order from Constantine, the ruler of the Romans, in the year 321 CE. It became a religion for them by the order of their rabbis.

The Friday prayer is the noon prayer (salat al-zuhr) of Friday, and it is not an extra prayer beyond the five daily prayers. Two rak'ahs were removed from the noon prayer because of the two sermons. It is narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "The Friday prayer was shortened only because of the sermon."

[Page 223]

I believe that this was a lightening upon people, since two sermons became obligatory on them along with the prayer, so each sermon was in the place of a rak'ah. This is the reason for sitting between the two sermons, as an indication that they stand in place of the two rak'ahs, and for this reason the sitting was brief. However, the two sermons were not given the rulings of the two rak'ahs, so the missing of one of them or the missing of both together does no harm, and it is not obligatory for the latecomer (masbuq) to make them up, nor is there a prostration for their omission, according to the majority of the jurists of the major cities. It is narrated from 'Ata', Mujahid, and Tawus that whoever misses the sermon on Friday prays four rak'ahs as the noon prayer. And from 'Ata': whoever catches one rak'ah of the Friday prayer adds three rak'ahs to it. He meant: if he misses the sermon and one rak'ah of the Friday prayer.

The recitation in the prayer was made aloud, although the norm for the daytime prayers is to recite quietly, for the benefit of making the people hear some surahs of the Qur'an, just as they were made to hear the sermon. So it was a prayer of guidance for the people of the town on one day of every week.

There is consensus that the Friday prayer stands in place of the noon prayer on Friday, so whoever prays it does not pray the noon prayer along with it. As for whoever did not pray it, due to an excuse or other reasons, it is obligatory upon him to pray the noon prayer. I saw in the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus that an imam stood to lead a congregation in the noon prayer after finishing the Friday prayer, and that is an innovation (bid'ah).

The jurists differed about the basic obligation at the time of the noon prayer on Friday. Malik, al-Shafi'i in his last of two opinions, Ahmad, and Zufar among the companions of Abu Hanifah said: the well-known Friday prayer is the obligation at the time of the zawal (midday) on Friday, and the noon prayer on that day is only a substitute for the Friday prayer, i.e., for one who did not pray the Friday prayer due to an excuse or the like.

Abu Hanifah, al-Shafi'i in his first opinion (which he retracted), Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad in one narration said: the obligation in origin is the noon prayer, and the Friday prayer is a substitute for the noon prayer. This is what the Hanafi jurists affirmed as correct.

Muhammad said in one narration from him: the obligation is one of the two prayers without specification, and the specification is for the mukallaf (responsible person), so it resembles the optional obligation (wajib mukhayyar), because in the optional obligation the doer of either of the two matters does not sin, while one who abandons the Friday prayer without an excuse is sinful.

[Page 224]

They said: the fruit of the disagreement appears in a free resident who prayed the noon prayer at the beginning of its time. Abu Hanifah and his companions said: he has the noon prayer absolutely, so that even if he went out after he had prayed the noon prayer, or did not go out, his obligation is not nullified. But according to Abu Hanifah his noon prayer is nullified merely by the act of striving (sa'y) absolutely, and according to his two companions his noon prayer is not nullified unless he catches the Friday prayer.

Malik and al-Shafi'i said: it is not permitted to pray the noon prayer on Friday, whether he catches the Friday prayer or not, whether he went out to it or not. That is, if he catches the Friday prayer the matter is clear, and if he does not catch it, it is obligatory upon him to pray another noon prayer.

The call to prayer (al-nida' li-l-salah) is the well-known adhan, which is the adhan for the noon prayer. It is reported in the Sahih from al-Sa'ib ibn Yazid, who said: "The call on Friday was when the imam sat on the minbar during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, and 'Umar. Al-Sa'ib ibn Yazid said: When 'Uthman came and the people in Medina increased, he added an adhan at al-Zawra'." (al-Zawra': a place in the market of Medina.) Some narrations describe it as the second adhan. The meaning of its being second is that it is a repeated adhan in addition to the original adhan, so it is second in legislation, and it does not mean that it is called after finishing the adhan that is called when the imam sits on the minbar. That is, it is called at the door of the mosque, since at that time people did not have a minaret. Some narrations describe it as the third call, and this is meant only because it is third when added to the first adhan. It does not mean that people call two adhans in the mosque; rather 'Uthman added it so that those on the outskirts of Medina would hear the call, and they sometimes called it the first adhan.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 62, verses 9–10 (part 2 of 2):

What appears from a careful examination of the reports is that this second adhan is called out immediately after the first adhan, because the purpose is for people to attend the prayer at one time. Some expressions in the reports and in the words of the narrators state that the adhan was called at al-Zawra' first, and then the imam would come out and the adhan would be given in front of him.

Ibn al-'Arabi said in al-'Aridah: When the people increased in number in the time of 'Uthman, he added a call at al-Zawra' so that the people would be aware of the time and begin to come to the Friday prayer. Then 'Uthman would come out, and when he sat on the minbar, the second adhan, which had been the first in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), was called, and then he would deliver the khutbah. Then the third adhan is called, meaning by it the iqamah. End of quote.

He also said in al-Ahkam: He called it, in the hadith of al-Sa'ib ibn Yazid, a "third," because it is an addition to the iqamah, so he made it the third of the iqamah; that is, because it was introduced after the iqamah had been legislated. He called the iqamah an adhan by way of similarity (mushakalah), or because it is a notification (iidhan) of entry into the prayer, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Between every two adhans there is a prayer for whoever wishes," meaning between the adhan and the iqamah. So people imagined that it was an original adhan, and they made the adhans three, and this was a delusion. Then they gathered them at one time, and this was a delusion upon a delusion. End of quote. Thus many people in the regions imagined that the adhan for the Friday prayer is three times. For this reason you see them calling three adhans in the mosques of Tunis, and this is an innovation (bid'ah).

Ibn al-'Arabi said in al-'Aridah: As for the Maghrib, meaning the lands of the Maghrib, three muezzins call the adhan there, due to the ignorance of the jurists. In al-Risalah: This second adhan was introduced by the Banu Umayyah, so he described it as the second, which is the verified position, but he attributed it to the Banu Umayyah because it is not established that the one who added it was 'Uthman. It was narrated by al-Bukhari and the authors of the Sunan from al-Sa'ib ibn Yazid, and Muslim did not narrate it, nor did Malik in the Muwatta'.

The reason for attributing it to the Banu Umayyah is that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, when he was in Kufa, did not call the adhan for the Friday prayer except a single adhan, as was the case in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the adhan which 'Uthman had introduced in Medina was abolished. Perhaps it was one of the caliphs of the Banu Umayyah who restored the second adhan. Malik said in al-Majmu'ah: Hisham ibn 'Abd al-Malik introduced a second adhan in front of him in the mosque.

Know that the call to which the command to strive (al-sa'y) in this verse is attached is the first call, and the second call was only a relaying of the adhan for those who were far away. Whoever hears it is obliged to strive to the Friday prayer, since he knows that a call for the Friday prayer has been made.

Al-sa'y: its original meaning is exerting oneself in walking. Here it is used for walking with eagerness and avoiding lateness, figuratively.

(Remembrance of Allah) has been interpreted as the prayer, and it has been interpreted as the khutbah. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and Sa'id ibn Jubayr explained it thus. Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: The correct view is that it includes all of it, its beginning being the khutbah.

I say: The choice of "remembrance of Allah" here, rather than saying "to the prayer," as in His saying ﴿Then when the prayer is concluded﴾, is so that both matters, the khutbah and the prayer, may be intended. In it is evidence for the obligation of the khutbah in the Friday prayer and its being a condition in general. The detailed rulings on neglecting the khutbah are not equal to those on neglecting the prayer, except in the basic prohibition of absenting oneself from attending the khutbah without an excuse.

In the hadith of the Muwatta': "When the imam comes out, the angels attend, listening to the remembrance (al-dhikr)." There is no doubt that when the imam comes out he begins with the khutbah, so the khutbah is part of the remembrance, and in this is an explanation of the word "remembrance" in this verse. They were forbidden from trading because it is what preoccupies them, and because the occasion of the revelation of the verse was that a group of them left the Friday prayer to go after a caravan of merchandise that had arrived, as will come in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And when they see a trade or amusement, they break away toward it﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 11].

Like trading is everything that preoccupies one from striving to the Friday prayer. And after trading and what is analogous to it, there has been disagreement concerning the annulment (naskh) of contracts that were concluded at the time of the Friday prayer. This is based on the disagreement over whether a prohibition necessitates the invalidity of what is prohibited. The position of Malik is that a prohibition necessitates invalidity unless there is an indication otherwise. Malik's statement in al-Mudawwanah: a sale concluded at the time of the Friday prayer between those upon whom the Friday prayer is obligatory is annulled. Al-Shafi'i said: it is not annulled, and he treated it like prayer in usurped land; this is also the view of Abu Hanifah.

As for a marriage contracted at the time of the Friday prayer: in al-'Utbiyyah from Ibn al-Qasim, it is not annulled. Perhaps he limited himself to what the prohibition was stated about in the Qur'an, and did not regard analogy as requiring the annulment of what is analogized. Likewise the leading Malikis said: a partnership, a gift, or a charity concluded at the time of the Friday prayer is not annulled, and they justified this by the rarity of the occurrence of their like, unlike sale.

The address of the verse is to all the believers, which indicates that the Friday prayer is obligatory upon each individual (fard 'ayn). A group deviated, saying it is obligatory as a communal duty (fard kifayah). Ibn al-Faras said: this was attributed to some Shafi'is. The Qur'anic address "O you who believe" is general, and the Sunnah has specified it by the non-obligation of the Friday prayer upon women, slaves, a traveler who arrives at a village where the Friday prayer is held, and whoever cannot make the effort to reach it.

The "min" in His saying (﴿from the day of Friday﴾) is partitive (tab'idiyyah), since the day of Friday is a time in which acts occur, among them the well-known prayer in it, so what occurs within the time is treated as parts of the thing. It is also permissible for "min" to be for location (zarfiyyah), like the one in His saying (﴿Show me what they have created from the earth﴾ [Fatir: 40]), meaning: in it, of earthly creatures.

The demonstrative "that" (dhalikum) refers to what has been mentioned, namely the command to strive to it and the command to leave off trading at that time; that is, that is better for you than what you gain from sales. The word "khayr" is a comparative form whose original is akhyar, its hamzah dropped due to frequent use.

The element compared against is omitted, being indicated by the context. The thing preferred is the prayer, meaning its reward. The thing compared against is the benefits of sale for seller and buyer.

It was followed by His saying, ﴿Then when the prayer is concluded, disperse in the land and seek of Allah's bounty﴾, to indicate that they have a span of the day which they may devote to sale and similar pursuits of livelihood, so they should not take that from the time of prayer and the remembrance of Allah. The command in ﴿disperse in the land and seek of Allah's bounty﴾ is for permission (ibahah).

What is meant by "Allah's bounty" is the earning of wealth and sustenance.

As for His saying, ﴿and remember Allah much﴾, it is a safeguard against being absorbed in the affairs of this world to the point of forgetting the remembrance of Allah or being distracted from the prayers, for success lies in devoting oneself to the pleasure of Allah, Exalted is He.

[p. 228]

It is coordinated with the clause ﴿When it is called for prayer on the day of Friday, then hasten to the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 9], and so on. The rebuke for abandoning what was commanded is coordinated with the mention of the command. In the coordinated clause the style of *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical address, here from third person to second person, that is, to the Prophet ﷺ) is used, to indicate that they deserve to have the address turned away from them, so they were deprived of the honour of being addressed. They are spoken of in the manner of absent persons, and this contains an allusion (*ta'ridh*) of rebuke.

The apparent form would have been: "When you see a trade or amusement, do not scatter toward it." Among the implications of expressing the speech contrary to its apparent form here is that this rebuke does not include all the believers, for a group of them remained with the Prophet ﷺ during his sermon and did not go out for trade or amusement.

In the authentic collection, on the authority of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, he said: "While we were praying with the Prophet ﷺ, and he was delivering the sermon on Friday, a caravan from Syria arrived carrying food, and the people turned toward it, until only twelve men remained with the Prophet ﷺ, I being among them." In another narration: "Among them were Abu Bakr and 'Umar, so Allah revealed concerning them this verse which is in al-Jumu'ah: ﴿And when they see a trade or amusement, they scatter toward it and leave you standing.﴾" End. They have mentioned in other narrations that there remained with the Prophet ﷺ Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman, 'Ali, Talhah, al-Zubayr, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, Abu 'Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, Sa'id ibn Zayd, Bilal, 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, 'Ammar ibn Yasir, and Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah; these are fourteen. al-Daraqutni mentioned in the hadith of Jabir that he said: "There were not with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ except forty men."

On the authority of Mujahid and Muqatil: "The Prophet ﷺ was delivering the sermon when Dihyah ibn Khalifah al-Kalbi arrived with merchandise, and his people met him with tambourines, so the people went out." In another narration, the people of Medina had suffered hunger and severe scarcity, so Dihyah arrived with merchandise of Syrian olive oil. In another narration: "[and food and other things], so the people went out of the mosque, fearing that they would be outdone in obtaining it." Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah said: "Whenever the young women were married, they were paraded with flutes and drums, and they scattered toward them. Therefore Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when they see a trade or amusement, they scatter toward it and leave you standing.﴾" It has been said that this occurred from them three times. There is no doubt that their going out was at times for the sake of the caravan and at times for the sake of the amusement.

It has been narrated that the caravan halted at a place called Ahjar al-Zayt (the Stones of Oil), so the narrator imagined and said: "with the merchandise of oil."

The pronoun in "toward it" (*ilayha*) refers to trade, because it was more important to them than amusement, and because the event on account of which the verse was revealed was the arrival of Dihyah's caravan from Syria. The pronoun for amusement was dispensed with by this, as in the verse of Qays ibn al-Khatim, or 'Amr ibn al-Harith ibn Imru' al-Qays:

*"We are content with what we have, and you are content with what you have, though opinions differ."*

Perhaps the division indicated by "or" (*aw*) in His saying ﴿or amusement﴾ is a division of the circumstances of those who scattered: some of them were men with families who went out to obtain provisions for their households, and some of them were youths who had no aspiration for provisions but loved to attend the amusement.

"*Idha*" (when) is a temporal adverb referring to past time, stripped of the meaning of a conditional, because this scattering has already occurred. It is not intended that they would return to it after this rebuke and what preceded it of command and exhortation. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿And when a matter of security or fear reaches them, they spread it around﴾ [al-Nisa': 83], and His saying: ﴿Nor [is there blame] upon those who came to you that you might mount them; you said, "I cannot find anything to mount you on," and they turned back﴾ [al-Tawbah: 92], and so on.

*Infidad* (scattering) is the intransitive form (*mutawi'*) of *faddahu*, meaning he dispersed it. Its use has become predominant for meanings other than the intransitive sense, that is, in an absolute sense, like "they dispersed." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They are the ones who say, "Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah until they disperse"﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 7].

His saying ﴿or amusement﴾ is for division, meaning: some of them scattered for the sake of trade, and some of them scattered for the sake of amusement. The feminine pronoun in His saying "toward it" (*ilayha*) is by way of giving precedence to the word "trade" (*tijarah*), because trade was the stronger motive for their scattering.

The clause ﴿and leave you standing﴾ is a severe censure of their action, since they neglected listening to the admonition of the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: they left you standing upon the pulpit. That was during the Friday sermon. The apparent sense is that it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: they left you in the state of admonition and guidance, so they wasted great knowledge by their scattering toward trade and amusement. This verse indicates the obligation of attending the sermon in the Friday prayer, since He did not say: "and they left the prayer."

Allah commanded His Prophet ﷺ to admonish them that what is with Allah of reward for attending the Friday prayer is better than the benefit of trade and the pleasure of amusement. Likewise, what Allah has prepared of provision for those who prefer obedience to Allah over that which distracts from it of means of livelihood is a recompense for them for their preference, a recompense in this world before the recompense of the Hereafter. Many a provision has not benefited the one who was greedy for it, even if it was abundant, and many a small provision benefits its possessor and returns to him with righteousness. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely reward them according to the best of what they used to do﴾ [al-Nahl: 97].

[p. 230]

He also said, relating the speech of Noah's people in general: ﴿So I said, "Seek forgiveness from your Lord; indeed, He is ever Forgiving. He will send [rain from] the sky upon you in abundance. And provide you with wealth and children and make for you gardens and make for you rivers"﴾ [Nuh: 10–12].

The speech is concluded with His saying ﴿And Allah is the best of providers﴾, because Allah provides provision for the one with whom He is pleased, free from troubles and sins, and because He provides the good of this world and the good of the Hereafter; none other than Allah is able to do that. People in this station are of varying ranks, which none knows but Allah, and He is the Knower of the hidden secrets.

Surah al-Munafiqun

This surah is named in the books of *sunnah* (prophetic traditions) and in books of *tafsir* (Qur'anic exegesis) "Surat al-Munafiqin" (The Surah of the Hypocrites), in view of the mention in it of their states and attributes.

This name occurs in the hadith of Zayd ibn Arqam in al-Tirmidhi, in his saying: "When we arose in the morning, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited Surat al-Munafiqin," and it will come shortly. al-Tabarani narrated in *al-Awsat* on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to recite in the Friday prayer Surat al-Jumu'ah, thereby exhorting the believers, and in the second rak'ah Surat al-Munafiqun, thereby rebuking the hypocrites."

It occurs in the Sahih of al-Bukhari and some books of tafsir as "Surat al-Munafiquna" (The Surah of "the Hypocrites ...") by way of quoting the word that occurs at its beginning, and it is similarly established in many Maghribi and Mashriqi copies of the Qur'an.

It is Medinan by consensus.

The counters agree that its verses number eleven.

It is counted the hundred and second (in the sequence of revelation) according to Jabir ibn Zayd. It was revealed after Surat al-Hajj and before Surat al-Mujadilah.

The correct view is that it was revealed during the expedition of the Banu al-Mustaliq. In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi there is a report from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that it was revealed during the expedition of Tabuk. In it there is also a report from Sufyan that this was in the expedition of the Banu al-Mustaliq; the expedition of the Banu al-Mustaliq was in the fifth year, and the expedition of Tabuk in the ninth year.

The scholars of the maghazi (military expeditions), Ibn al-'Arabi in *al-'Aridah*, and Ibn Kathir preferred that it was revealed during the expedition of the Banu al-Mustaliq, and this is the more evident view, because the saying of 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, "The mightier will surely expel the meaner from it," suits the time when the affair of the hypocrites had not yet weakened, whereas their affair was in weakness every day. The expedition of Tabuk was at the end of the years of prophethood, and by then the affair of the hypocrites had weakened.

The occasion of its revelation is what has been narrated on the authority of Zayd ibn Arqam: "He said: We were on a campaign, and a man from the Muhajirun struck a man from the Juhayni, an ally of the Ansar, on the buttocks. The Juhayni said: 'O Ansar!' and the Muhajiri said: 'O Muhajirun!' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ heard that and said: 'What is this call of the Jahiliyyah (Age of Ignorance)?' They said: 'A man from the Muhajirun struck a man from the Ansar.' He said: 'Leave it, for it is putrid' (that is, abandon the call of the Jahiliyyah: 'O such-and-such!'). 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy heard this report and said: 'Have they actually done it? By Allah, if we return to Medina, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it.' And he said: 'Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah until they disperse from around him.' Zayd ibn Arqam said: I heard that, so I informed my uncle, and he mentioned it to the Prophet ﷺ. He summoned me, and I related it to him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions, and they swore that they had not said it. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ declared me a liar, and he believed him. A grief came upon me such as had never come upon me before. My uncle said: 'You intended nothing except that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ should declare you a liar.'" In another narration: "... until he declared you a liar. When we arose in the morning, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited Surat al-Munafiqun, and said to me: 'Indeed Allah has confirmed you.'"

In a narration of al-Tirmidhi concerning this hadith: that the Muhajiri was a Bedouin, and that the Ansari was among the companions of 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, and that the Muhajiri struck the Ansari on his head with a piece of wood and wounded him, and that 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy said: "Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah until they disperse from around him," meaning the Bedouins. The people of the biographies (*siyar*) mentioned that the Muhajiri, from Ghifar, was named Jahjah, a hired man of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab; and that the Ansari, a Juhani, was named Sinan, an ally of Ibn Ubayy. Then it is possible that the incident was one event. The narrator from Zayd ibn Arqam was inconsistent in describing it, and it is possible that two incidents occurred in one campaign.

al-Wahidi mentioned in *Asbab al-Nuzul* (Occasions of Revelation): "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and said to him: 'You are the author of this speech which has reached me.' 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy said: 'By Him who revealed the Book to you, I did not say anything of this, and Zayd is indeed a liar.'"

The apparent sense is that Ibn Ubayy uttered the first saying in a fit of anger, to stir up his people; then he feared the exposure of his hypocrisy, so he denied it.

As for the second saying, Zayd ibn Arqam included it in his narration, and Ibn Ubayy uttered it in the manner of a counsellor, as will come in the explanation of its quotation.

According to the more correct view, it was revealed before Surat al-Ahzab. On the view that it was revealed during the expedition of Tabuk, it would have been revealed along with Surat Bara'ah (al-Tawbah), or shortly before it, and that is far-fetched.

\* \* \*

The surah exposes the states of the hypocrites by enumerating many of their inner traits, some of which arise from others: lying, breaking the covenant of Allah, instability in belief, baseness of souls within bodies that dazzle and impress, and insistence on turning away from seeking the truth and guidance, and on barring people from it. Each section of the surah's verses that opens with "*idha*" (when) is devoted to one of these purposes. You have already learned that the reference here was to the denial by 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul of what he had sworn regarding his disavowal of what he had said.

It concludes with an admonition to the believers and an exhortation to spend and to store up provision for the Hereafter before the appointed term arrives.
